body:
Establishment of Mughal Rule in India

The Mughal Empire was established in northern India by Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur in 1526. It gradually developed into a large empire whose rulers combined military conquest with administrative organisation and alliances with regional powers.

Babur belonged to the Timurid ruling tradition of Central Asia. He traced his paternal ancestry to Timur and his maternal ancestry to Genghis Khan. After losing control of his Central Asian homeland, he established himself at Kabul in 1504 and subsequently turned towards northern India.

Babur's Major Battles

Babur's victory at Panipat gave him control of Delhi and Agra, but he still had to overcome powerful regional opponents. His principal Indian campaigns were:

  • First Battle of Panipat, 1526: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan of the Lodi dynasty. This victory established Mughal rule in Delhi and Agra. Babur used field artillery and firearms effectively, alongside cavalry tactics.
  • Battle of Khanwa, 1527: Babur defeated the forces of Rana Sanga of Mewar and his allies. This strengthened Mughal authority against an important Rajput coalition.
  • Battle of Chanderi, 1528: Babur defeated the Rajput forces associated with Medini Rai, further consolidating his position in northern India.

Babur used gunpowder weapons effectively at Panipat, but he did not introduce gunpowder or firearms to India for the first time. These technologies were already known in parts of the subcontinent.

Humayun: Loss and Recovery of the Empire

Humayun succeeded Babur in 1530. He faced challenges from Afghan rulers and difficulties arising from rival claims within the Mughal family. His principal opponent was Sher Khan, who later became known as Sher Shah Suri.

  • Battle of Chausa, 1539: Sher Khan defeated Humayun.
  • Battle of Kanauj, 1540: Sher Shah defeated Humayun again, forcing him to lose control of his Indian territories.
  • 1540–1555: The Sur rulers controlled the principal Mughal territories in northern India. Humayun eventually obtained assistance from Safavid Iran.
  • 1555: Humayun recovered Delhi and restored Mughal rule.
  • 1556: Humayun died, and his son Akbar succeeded him.

The Sur interlude is important because Mughal rule was interrupted between Humayun's defeat and restoration. The Mughal dynasty had been founded in 1526, but continuous Mughal control of Delhi was not maintained throughout the following decades.

Why Mughal Succession Was Often Contested

The Mughals did not consistently follow primogeniture, the rule under which the eldest son inherits the ruler's position. Timurid traditions recognised claims to a share of the family inheritance among sons. The imperial throne, however, could not be effectively divided among competing claimants.

As a result, Mughal princes frequently competed for supreme power. Humayun faced difficulties involving his brothers, while later emperors also experienced rebellions and succession struggles. The absence of a fixed rule identifying the next emperor made the support of nobles and military forces particularly important.

Prelims focus

  • 1526, First Panipat: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
  • 1527, Khanwa: Babur defeated Rana Sanga and his allies.
  • 1528, Chanderi: Babur defeated the Rajput forces associated with Medini Rai.
  • 1539 and 1540: Humayun was defeated at Chausa and Kanauj respectively.
  • 1555: Humayun recovered Delhi; Akbar succeeded him in 1556.
  • Trap: The First Battle of Panipat involved Ibrahim Lodi, not Hemu, who was defeated in the Second Battle of Panipat.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, pp. 46–50, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Theme 9, Kings and Chronicles, pp. 224–226; NIOS, Senior Secondary History (315), Lesson 10, Establishment of the Mughal Rule, sections on Babur, Humayun and Sher Shah, consulted 19 November 2026.]

body:
Akbar's Accession and the Second Battle of Panipat

Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605. He became emperor at approximately 13 years of age following Humayun's death. His accession took place at Kalanaur in Punjab, and Bairam Khan initially acted as his regent.

Akbar inherited an insecure kingdom. Afghan political forces remained influential, and control of Delhi was challenged by Hemu, also known as Hem Chandra, who had served under the Sur rulers.

In the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556, the Mughal forces defeated Hemu. Bairam Khan exercised leadership during this early period of Akbar's reign. The victory secured Mughal control over Delhi and helped establish the political foundation for Akbar's subsequent expansion.

Bairam Khan's regency lasted from 1556 to 1560. After taking personal control of government, Akbar strengthened his authority over powerful nobles and undertook campaigns against neighbouring kingdoms.

Principal Campaigns under Akbar

Akbar expanded through a combination of warfare, negotiated submission and the incorporation of local ruling groups into imperial service. His campaigns can be understood in three broad stages.

Consolidation in Northern and Central India

  • Malwa, 1561: Mughal forces defeated Baz Bahadur, the ruler of Malwa.
  • Gondwana, 1564: Mughal forces campaigned against Gondwana, associated with Rani Durgavati.
  • Chittor, 1568: Akbar captured the important fortress of Chittor, then associated with the Sisodiya kingdom of Mewar.
  • Ranthambhor, 1569: The Mughal capture of this major fort further strengthened their position in Rajasthan.

These victories increased Mughal territorial control, but the capture of a fortress did not necessarily mean that all resistance in the surrounding kingdom had ended. The Sisodiya rulers of Mewar continued to oppose Mughal authority.

Expansion into Gujarat and Eastern India

Akbar's Gujarat campaign of 1572–1573 brought an important western region under Mughal control. The campaign included the occupation of Ahmedabad and Surat. Local opposition continued, and Akbar returned to suppress a rebellion in Gujarat in 1573.

Gujarat mattered to the Mughal Empire because it connected the inland political centres of northern India with major centres of trade and the western seaboard. Its incorporation strengthened the empire's territorial and commercial position.

The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri commemorates Akbar's victory in Gujarat. It provides a useful connection between a military event in Gujarat and an imperial monument in northern India.

After the Gujarat campaigns, Mughal operations in the east brought Bihar and Bengal increasingly under imperial control during the 1570s, with the struggle against Afghan power continuing through the decade.

North-Western and Deccan Expansion

In the later part of his reign, Akbar directed attention towards the north-western frontier, where the empire confronted the interests of the Uzbeks and Safavids. Mughal authority was extended over Kashmir, Kabul and Qandahar.

Campaigns also began in the Deccan. By the end of Akbar's reign, the empire had obtained Berar, Khandesh and parts of Ahmadnagar. The entire Deccan was not conquered under Akbar; powerful kingdoms such as Bijapur and Golconda remained outside direct Mughal control.

Akbar's success depended on more than victories in battle. He also secured the cooperation of regional rulers and placed officers of different backgrounds within a common imperial administration.

Prelims focus

  • 1556, Second Panipat: Akbar's Mughal forces defeated Hemu during Bairam Khan's regency.
  • 1561: Malwa campaign against Baz Bahadur.
  • 1564: Gondwana campaign associated with Rani Durgavati.
  • 1568 and 1569: Chittor and Ranthambhor were captured respectively.
  • 1572–1573: Akbar's Gujarat conquest; Buland Darwaza commemorates this victory.
  • Trap: Capturing Chittor did not end Sisodiya resistance in Mewar.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, pp. 47–49; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Theme 9, Kings and Chronicles, pp. 225 and 236; NIOS, Senior Secondary History (315), Lesson 10, Establishment of the Mughal Rule, section 10.4, consulted 19 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Fatehpur Sikri, historical description, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Akbar's Accession, Imperial Expansion and the Conquest of Gujarat

body:
The Principal Mughal Emperors

The Mughal Empire expanded and developed through the reigns of several rulers. For preliminary examinations, the sequence from Babur to Aurangzeb and the principal events associated with each emperor form the chronological foundation.

EmperorReignPrincipal association
Babur1526–1530Foundation of Mughal rule after First Panipat
Humayun1530–1540; 1555–1556Loss of empire to the Sur rulers and recovery of Delhi
Akbar1556–1605Territorial expansion and administrative consolidation
Jahangir1605–1627Continuation of Akbar's institutions and settlement with Mewar
Shah Jahan1628–1658Deccan campaigns and conflict over succession
Aurangzeb1658–1707Annexation of Bijapur and Golconda; prolonged regional resistance

Humayun's two reign periods are separated by the Sur interlude. Jahangir died in 1627, while Shah Jahan's reign is conventionally dated from his accession in 1628. The dates should therefore not be treated as a continuously numbered sequence without transitional periods.

Jahangir: Continuity and the Mewar Settlement

Jahangir succeeded Akbar in 1605. He continued many of the political and administrative arrangements established by his father. Mughal campaigns against regional powers also continued.

An important event was the 1615 settlement with Amar Singh of Mewar. The Sisodiya rulers had resisted Mughal authority for decades. The settlement brought Mewar into a relationship with the Mughal emperor while allowing the ruling house to retain a significant degree of dignity and local authority.

The agreement illustrates how the empire could achieve political submission through negotiation when prolonged military conflict had not produced a lasting settlement.

Shah Jahan: Campaigns and a Succession Crisis

Shah Jahan ruled from 1628 to 1658. He continued Mughal efforts to consolidate power in the Deccan. Ahmadnagar was brought under Mughal control, and agreements with Bijapur and Golconda in 1636 recognised Mughal influence without immediately incorporating those kingdoms into the empire.

In the north-west, Mughal efforts to extend or preserve authority were less successful. Campaigns towards Balkh did not establish lasting control, and Qandahar was lost to the Safavids.

When Shah Jahan became seriously ill in 1657, his sons struggled for the throne. Aurangzeb emerged victorious in the succession conflict of 1657–1658. His brother Dara Shukoh was defeated and later executed. Shah Jahan was confined in Agra, and Aurangzeb became emperor in 1658.

The Mughal throne did not automatically pass to the eldest son. Shah Jahan's succession crisis shows the difference between a prince having a claim to the throne and actually securing imperial authority.

Aurangzeb: The Deccan and Continuing Resistance

Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 to 1707. The empire reached its greatest territorial extent during his reign, especially through campaigns in the Deccan. Yet the expansion also required prolonged military expenditure and efforts to control distant territories.

  • Maratha resistance: Mughal campaigns against Shivaji and later Maratha forces did not establish lasting peace. Shivaji escaped from Mughal custody at Agra in 1666, and resistance continued.
  • Bijapur, 1686: Aurangzeb annexed the Bijapur Sultanate following a sustained campaign.
  • Golconda, 1687: The Golconda Sultanate was annexed the following year.
  • Other resistance: Mughal authority faced challenges from the Ahoms in the north-east, Sikhs, Jats and Satnamis in northern India, and sections of the Rajputs.

The annexation of Bijapur and Golconda removed two independent Deccan sultanates, but it did not end warfare in the Deccan. Prolonged conflict with the Marathas continued to consume imperial resources.

Why Expansion Did Not Guarantee Stability

Military conquest could enlarge the territory claimed by the emperor, but effective rule required dependable officers, revenue collection, local cooperation and secure communication. When campaigns became prolonged, the state had to maintain large forces and support officials across distant regions.

By the later years of Aurangzeb's reign, continuing wars and tensions over revenue assignments placed increasing pressure on the imperial system. Following his death in 1707, succession disputes and the growing strength of regional powers weakened central Mughal authority.

Prelims focus

  • Jahangir: 1605–1627; settlement with Amar Singh of Mewar in 1615.
  • Shah Jahan: 1628–1658; Deccan agreements with Bijapur and Golconda in 1636.
  • 1657–1658: Succession conflict ending in Aurangzeb's victory.
  • Aurangzeb: 1658–1707; Bijapur annexed in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.
  • 1707: Death of Aurangzeb, followed by renewed succession conflict.
  • Trap: Agreements with Bijapur and Golconda under Shah Jahan were not the same as their later annexation under Aurangzeb.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, pp. 48–50 and 52; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Theme 9, Kings and Chronicles, pp. 225–226; NIOS, Senior Secondary History (315), Lesson 10, Establishment of the Mughal Rule, section 10.4, consulted 19 November 2026; IGNOU, Ahmednagar, Bijapur and Golkonda, Unit 8, 2017, sections on Mughal campaigns and the annexations, consulted 19 November 2026.]
